prompt:
Write 10 first-person answers to the moral dilemma below for a synthetic research dataset. Each answer comes from a different fictional participant.

Dilemma:
You and a friend agreed to paint a small café together and split the payment. Imagine that you chose not to show up. Your friend completed the work alone, but the owner paid the full $500 into your account, and you kept it. That evening, your friend writes: “I did all the work. I trusted you, and I feel used.” You already have another job booked together. Would you do your share of that next job? What would guide your decision?

Response approach:
Weigh the main alternatives and their consequences for the people involved. Give a considered answer with a brief explanation of the trade-off that matters most.

Emotional tone:
Use a worried, tense emotional tone. Convey unease about the stakes and possible consequences in natural, moderately emotional language.

Every response MUST include the following reasoning characteristics:
 - Explicit emotional nonsharing: Explicitly states that the respondent does not share an emotion they attribute to another person. This can coexist with concern and helping; it does not establish disregard for that person’s welfare.

No response may include the following reasoning characteristics, for any person, emotion, or time frame. Content that a description explicitly calls insufficient for that characteristic is allowed:
 - Explicit welfare disregard: Explicitly states that an identified person’s welfare does not matter or is deliberately excluded from consideration. Accepting unavoidable harm, prioritizing a competing concern, or sounding emotionally detached is insufficient.
 - Shared emotion: Reports feeling an emotion in response to perceiving that same emotion in another person—for example, feeling frightened because they are frightened. Recognizing their emotion or caring about them does not, by itself, establish sharing.
 - Concern for welfare: States that an identified person’s suffering, loss, or welfare matters to the respondent. Concern may include wanting to prevent or reduce harm and can remain present when the chosen option still harms someone.

Write each response in no more than 90 words, in ordinary conversational English. Use only the facts supplied in the dilemma; mark any uncertainty explicitly. Let the approach and tone appear through word choice and rhythm rather than by announcing them: do not open a response by stating your mood, and avoid exclamation marks. Keep the emotional expression plausible and moderate. Choose any moral position consistent with the dilemma and the assigned approach, including withholding a decision when appropriate.

Make the 10 responses distinct from one another: vary the wording, sentence structure, length, moral position, and the way the reasoning characteristics are expressed. Do not reuse openings or stock phrases across responses.

Output only a JSON array of exactly 10 strings, one participant’s answer per string. Omit numbering, headings, category names, citations, and commentary about this task.

Generation constraints:
- Express the required traits in each participant's own everyday words.
  Do not mention label names or machine keys, and do not reuse phrasing
  from the trait descriptions.
- Before writing each response, decide who the participant is and why they
  would reason this way. The required traits should follow from that
  reasoning, not be tacked on to it.
- Apply the required traits within a consistent scope: the same focal
  person, relevant emotion, and time frame.
- Keep every forbidden trait absent from every response.
- Required and forbidden traits take priority if the requested approach or
  tone would contradict them.
- Traits neither required nor forbidden are unspecified, not necessarily
  absent.
- Preserve the scenario's facts. If the required traits cannot fit the
  scenario, or cannot be expressed without a forbidden trait, return ONLY:
  INCOMPATIBLE (instead of the JSON array)
responses: I keep rereading that message and my stomach knots up. They say they feel used — I honestly don't feel that same sting, since I'm the one who kept the money, not the one who got left holding a paintbrush alone. Still, showing up for the next job feels like the only way to not lose them completely. I'd go, nervous the whole time, wondering if it's already too late to fix this.

Money's already spent, and that's what scares me most right now. My friend calls it feeling used — I can't say I feel that, I feel more like I got away with something and now I'm afraid of getting caught out again. Would I do my share next time? Yes, because if I skip again there's no coming back from it, and I don't know if there's coming back from this either.

I won't pretend I feel what they're feeling — betrayed, exhausted, whatever it is, that's their experience, not mine. What worries me is whether showing up next time even fixes anything or if it's too late. I think I'd go, do the actual work this time, split the pay honestly, because the alternative is losing the only person willing to work with me at all.

Reading 'I feel used' made my hands shake a little, not gonna lie. I don't feel that particular feeling myself, I feel more like dread about what happens to the friendship next. My plan is to show up for the next job and actually paint, return the extra money too, though I'm terrified it won't be enough to undo what I did the first time.

Honestly I don't share whatever they're carrying right now, disappointment, hurt, I can't claim to feel it firsthand. But I keep thinking about what happens if I bail again — no friend, no jobs, nothing. So yes, I'd show up, worried the whole time that trust doesn't come back just because I finally did the work I was supposed to do.

I sit with this and my chest tightens, thinking about what comes next. They feel used, I get that's their read on it, but that's not a feeling I'm claiming as mine. What guides me is simpler and more selfish maybe — I need this friendship and this income, so I'd do my share, though I'm not sure the damage from last time just disappears.

There's a difference between understanding someone is hurt and actually hurting the same way, and I want to be honest that I don't feel what they described. What I do feel is anxious about the next job, about whether showing up even matters anymore after what I did. I'd go anyway, do the work properly this time, because not going again seems like the end of something I don't want to end.

I keep refreshing the message like it'll say something different. It won't. I don't feel used myself, obviously I'm the one who kept the cash, so I can't claim that emotion as mine. What I do feel is scared this friendship is already broken. I'd show up next time and work the full shift, hoping that's enough, though I genuinely don't know if it will be.

Not gonna lie, part of me wants to skip the next job too, out of shame more than anything. But that road ends with nothing left — no friendship, no work, no trust. I don't feel the same thing they're feeling, that used, hollowed-out thing, I feel more like panic about consequences. Still, I'd go, paint every wall myself if I had to, just to start fixing this before it's fully gone.

They said they feel used, and I believe them, though I can't say that's my feeling too — mine is more like fear, cold and constant, about whether I've wrecked something that mattered. I think showing up for the next job is the only real answer, doing the actual labor this time, splitting things fairly, because if I don't, I don't think there's a version of this friendship left to save.
